title: Chapter 5 Quiz
description: Test your knowledge of scripting basics, Debug.Log, movement, and public variables!

questions.question: What language does Unity use for scripting?
questions.explanation: C# is the primary scripting language for Unity.

questions.question: How do you create a new C# script?
options: Right‑click in Project window → Create → C# Script
questions.explanation: Scripts are created from the Project window context menu.

questions.question: A script file name must match the class name inside the script.
questions.explanation: Unity requires the file name and the main class name to be identical.

questions.question: What does 'using UnityEngine;' do?
options: It imports the Unity engine library so you can use its classes
It makes the script run faster
It is optional and does nothing
questions.explanation: 'using UnityEngine;' gives access to classes like GameObject, Transform, Debug, etc.

questions.question: What does the `: MonoBehaviour` part mean in the class definition?
options: The script inherits from MonoBehaviour, allowing it to be a component
questions.explanation: MonoBehaviour is the base class that makes scripts attachable to GameObjects.

questions.question: When does the Start() method run?
questions.explanation: Start() is called once after the script is enabled, before any Update calls.

questions.question: Which method runs once per frame?
questions.explanation: Update() is called every frame; use it for continuous logic.

questions.question: What is the purpose of Debug.Log()?
options: To print messages to the Console
questions.explanation: Debug.Log() outputs information to the Console window for debugging.

questions.question: To print a warning message, you use Debug.Log_____.
questions.explanation: The method is Debug.LogWarning().

questions.question: What does `transform.Translate(0, 0, 1)` do?
options: Moves the object 1 unit along its local Z axis
questions.explanation: Translate moves the object by the given offset in local space.

questions.question: Why should you multiply movement by `Time.deltaTime`?
options: To stop the object from moving
questions.explanation: Multiplying by deltaTime ensures constant speed regardless of frame rate.

questions.question: `Time.deltaTime` is the time since the game started.
questions.explanation: Time.deltaTime is the time since the last frame, not total time. Total time is `Time.time`.

questions.question: At 60 FPS, approximately what is the value of Time.deltaTime?
questions.explanation: 1 / 60 ≈ 0.0167 seconds per frame.

questions.question: How do you expose a private variable to the Inspector?
questions.explanation: [SerializeField] makes a private field visible in the Inspector.

questions.question: What data type is suitable for a speed value like 3.5?
questions.explanation: float holds decimal numbers. int holds whole numbers.

questions.question: Public variables can be edited in the Inspector during Play mode.
questions.explanation: Yes, public fields are editable in real‑time during Play mode for testing.

questions.question: What happens to Inspector changes made during Play mode after you stop?
options: They are saved to the script
They are lost (revert to pre‑play values)
questions.explanation: Changes during Play mode are temporary and discarded upon stopping.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a valid C# variable declaration?
questions.explanation: The string value 'Hero' must be in quotes. Correct: `string name = "Hero";`

questions.question: What does `transform.Translate(moveDirection * speed * Time.deltaTime);` do?
options: Moves the object in the direction of moveDirection at a constant speed
Teleports the object to a new position
questions.explanation: It moves the object in the given direction, scaled by speed and time, for smooth movement.

questions.question: Which of the following is a correct way to print a variable to the Console?
questions.explanation: You concatenate the string and variable, or use string interpolation.

questions.question: What happens if you attach the same script to two different GameObjects?
options: Each GameObject gets its own instance of the script
questions.explanation: Each GameObject runs its own independent copy of the script component.

questions.question: You can have multiple scripts attached to the same GameObject.
questions.explanation: A single GameObject can have many script components, each adding different behavior.
